label: RCA Victor
rationale: Ellington's late-period masterpiece and the load-bearing statement of his 1960s orchestra — the record that most completely answers 'why the Ellington band still mattered after bebop.' Consensus is the strongest signal here: The Penguin Guide to Jazz rates it four stars out of four and names it 'a postwar peak' (S1 citing Cook & Morton, 2010), singling out 'Isfahan' as 'arguably the most beautiful item in Ellington's and Strayhorn's entire output'; DownBeat gave it five stars (S1); and it won the 1968 Grammy for Best Instrumental Jazz Performance – Large Group (S1). The suite is a defining statement of the Ellington–Strayhorn partnership — recorded December 1966, months before Strayhorn's death, it is the last album of new Strayhorn material Ellington recorded in Strayhorn's lifetime (S1). Session gravity is absolute: the full late-period orchestra in peak form — Hodges, Gonsalves, Carney, Hamilton, Cootie Williams, Cat Anderson, Lawrence Brown — a personnel network that is itself the core of the big-band canon. It still plays: 'Isfahan' became a standard, and the suite's coloristic writing has made it the most studied and re-recorded Ellington work of the period (Anthony Brown's 1999 Asian-American Orchestra re-recording, S1). The canon currently holds only Money Jungle (Ellington's 1962 trio side); the orchestra — the instrument Ellington actually led — is represented by no defining suite, which is a visible hole a jazz listener would notice.
consensus: Penguin Guide 4/4 stars ('a postwar peak', Cook & Morton 2010); DownBeat 5 stars (Morgenstern 1967); 1968 Grammy, Best Instrumental Jazz Performance – Large Group; AllMusic 'quite essential' (Yanow).

personnel_record.notes: Recorded December 19-21, 1966 at RCA Victor's Studio A, New York City (S3; S2 confirms the Dec 19-21 window and New York). Nine compositions, all by Ellington and Billy Strayhorn except 'Ad Lib on Nippon' by Ellington alone (S1). Strayhorn died May 1967, so this is one of the last albums recorded in his lifetime to feature his compositions (S1). Producer: Brad McCuen per the Toronto Public Library/BiblioCommons catalog (S5); Wikipedia's infobox prints 'Brad McKuen', recorded here as a name variant — McCuen is the documented spelling. Engineer not named in any consulted source — recorded null, epistemic unk. Full orchestra plays throughout; featured solos rotate per track (S1): Tourist Point of View (Gonsalves), Bluebird of Delhi/Mynah (Hamilton, clarinet), Isfahan (Hodges), Mount Harissa (Gonsalves & Ellington), Blue Pepper (Hodges & Cat Anderson), Agra (Carney), Amad (Lawrence Brown), Ad Lib on Nippon (Ellington & Hamilton). The 1995 reissue added four alternate takes (bonus tracks) — excluded from the track list here per the original-release convention.

scope_check.boundary_note: Style-lineage boundary in play per one reference: late-period orchestral Ellingtonia versus the canon's post-bebop/hard-bop center; not a hard window or excluded-style gate.

ballot.case_for: The consensus case is overwhelming and independent: Penguin Guide 4/4 as a 'postwar peak,' DownBeat five stars, the 1968 Grammy for large-group jazz, and AllMusic 'quite essential' (S1). It is the defining late Ellington–Strayhorn suite, recorded December 1966 months before Strayhorn's death, with 'Isfahan' entering the standard repertoire and Anthony Brown's 1999 Asian-American Orchestra re-recording as lineage evidence (S1). Session gravity is absolute—Hodges, Gonsalves, Carney, Hamilton, Cootie Williams, Cat Anderson, Lawrence Brown—and the canon's only current Ellington holding is the small-group Money Jungle, leaving his actual orchestra without a defining suite.
ballot.case_against: The strongest against-case is a scope objection, not quality: this is Ellington's swing-era-derived orchestral idiom extended into 1967, not the small-group post-bebop language at the canon's center, so it needs John's boundary ruling rather than automatic inclusion. Sourcing depth also thins the otherwise strong consensus: the Penguin/DownBeat/Grammy claims rest largely on the Wikipedia relay in S1 rather than separate critical or sessionographic sources, and the engineer is unk. A lesser argument is that other late suites like ...And His Mother Called Him Bill could compete for the definitive late-orchestral slot, though consensus generally favors Far East Suite.
ballot.disagreement: Reference 1 tiered this scope_call, arguing a real style-lineage boundary is in play; Reference 2 tiered consensus_core and saw no style boundary, treating it as firmly within the post-bebop timeline. The split is over whether late orchestral Ellington is continuous with the canon's post-bebop center or a separate carryover, not over quality or priority.
ballot.recommendation: John should rule explicitly on the late-orchestral Ellington scope boundary; if ruled in scope, this is a must-have defining statement.
